text: This lesson covers PL-SQL collections — and there are three real, distinct types here, not one generic concept: V-array, nested table, and associative array. Each behaves differently, and none of them map cleanly onto a single T-SQL construct.

First, the V-array — variable-size array. It declares its maximum size right up front, five here, and it can never hold more elements than that. It's the most array-like of the three: densely indexed from one, with a hard ceiling you decide at declaration time. Reach for it when you know the data genuinely has a small, fixed upper bound.

A nested table has no upper bound at all — it grows as needed. And here's the capability a V-array doesn't have: a nested table type can actually be used as a real column type in a database table, letting a single row store a variable-length collection directly. That's an Oracle-specific feature with no V-array equivalent.

The associative array, formerly called a PL-SQL table, is indexed by either an integer or, as shown here, a string — and it exists only in memory, as a purely PL-SQL construct, with no database column type at all. Indexing by string is what makes this one feel like a dictionary or hash map, and it's the collection you'll reach for most often in ordinary procedural code.

Now, where does T-SQL fit in? Nowhere close, actually. A T-SQL table variable is a real database-engine row set, with its own storage and optimizer involvement — fundamentally different from an in-memory PL-SQL collection. There's no T-SQL analogue to a string-keyed collection variable, and no equivalent of a V-array's fixed-size-at-declaration semantics either.

Next lesson: autonomous transactions — a genuinely unique PL-SQL capability for committing or rolling back independently of whatever transaction called you, something T-SQL's nested transactions flatly cannot do. See you there.
